summary: Describes how link-state and Traffic Engineering information, normally spread by IGP routing protocols, can be collected from a network and shared with outside components using BGP. It is the BGP Link-State (BGP-LS) specification and replaces RFC 7752 and RFC 9029.

plainLanguage.summary: Inside a network, the routing protocol already knows every link and how much capacity each one has. This document lets that same information travel over BGP, so a path computation server or an ALTO server outside the network can see it. A router publishes its own topology as BGP routes, and the pieces are gathered and handed to the tools that need them.

questions: how does bgp-ls carry link-state information
what are bgp-ls producer propagator and consumer
what afi and safi does bgp-ls use
subtitle: Carrying a network's link-state and traffic engineering information over BGP, so tools outside it can compute paths.

tldr.problem: Link-state and traffic engineering information normally stays inside one routing area, so a tool outside that area cannot compute end-to-end paths across it.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a BGP address family and an encoding format that carry nodes, links and prefixes as BGP routes, with their properties in a separate BGP path attribute.
tldr.outcome: This replaces RFC 7752 and folds in the updates from RFC 9029. It gives path computation elements and ALTO servers a single feed of topology, and it lets an operator hide or aggregate parts of the network.

today: RFC 9552 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of BGP-LS. It replaced RFC 7752 by completely rewriting it, and it also absorbed the updates that RFC 9029 had made to RFC 7752.

sections.title: Why Link-State Information Leaves the IGP
sections.content:
The contents of a Link-State Database or of an IGP's Traffic Engineering Database describe only the links and nodes within an IGP area. Some applications, such as end-to-end Traffic Engineering, would benefit from visibility outside one area or Autonomous System to make better decisions.

The IETF has defined the Path Computation Element as a mechanism for computing end-to-end TE paths that cross the visibility of more than one TED or that require CPU-intensive or coordinated computations. It has also defined the ALTO server as an entity that generates an abstracted network topology and provides it to network-aware applications. Both need to gather information about the topologies and capabilities of the network.

This document describes a mechanism by which link-state and TE information can be collected from networks and shared with external components using BGP. It is achieved using a BGP Network Layer Reachability Information encoding format. The mechanism applies to physical and virtual, for example tunnel, IGP links, and it is subject to policy control.

A router maintains one or more databases for storing link-state information about nodes and links in any given area. Link attributes stored in these databases include local and remote IP addresses, local and remote interface identifiers, link IGP metric, link TE metric, link bandwidth, reservable bandwidth, per Class-of-Service class reservation state, preemption, and Shared Risk Link Groups. The router's BGP-LS process can retrieve topology from these databases and distribute it to a consumer, either directly or via a peer BGP Speaker, typically a dedicated route reflector.

A BGP Speaker may apply a configurable policy to the information that it distributes. It may distribute the real physical topology, or it may create an abstracted topology where virtual, aggregated nodes are connected by virtual paths. Aggregated nodes can be created, for example, out of multiple routers in a Point of Presence. The BGP Speaker can also apply policy to determine when information is updated, so that there is a reduction in information flow from the network to the consumers.
sections.plainLanguage: A router already knows its neighbourhood in detail: which links exist, how fast they are and how much spare capacity they have. That knowledge normally stops at the edge of the area. This document lets it travel outwards over BGP, so a central server can plan paths across the whole network.

sections.title: The Three BGP-LS Roles
sections.content:
The BGP Speakers in the collection and distribution model can be seen playing different roles, and the document introduces terms for them that are used throughout.

The BGP-LS Producer is a BGP Speaker that is originating link-state information into BGP. Speakers R1, R2 to Rn originate link-state information from their underlying link-state IGP protocols into BGP-LS. If R1 and R2 are in the same IGP flooding domain, they would ordinarily originate the same link-state information. R1 may also originate information from sources other than IGP, for example its local node information.

The BGP-LS Consumer is a consumer application or process, not a BGP Speaker. The communication of information MUST be unidirectional, from a BGP Speaker to the consumer application, and a consumer MUST NOT be able to send information to a BGP Speaker for origination into BGP-LS.

The BGP-LS Propagator is a BGP Speaker that is performing BGP protocol processing on the link-state information. It handles BGP-LS UPDATE messages and performs the BGP Decision Process as part of deciding what information is to be propagated.

These roles are not mutually exclusive. The same BGP Speaker may be the Producer for some link-state information and the Propagator for other information, while also providing it to a Consumer.
sections.plainLanguage: Three jobs are involved. A producer takes its own router's view of the network and puts it into BGP. A propagator relays that information across the BGP network, applying the usual BGP rules about what to pass on. A consumer is the program that actually wants the topology, such as a path computation server.

sections.title: The TLV Format
sections.content:
Information in the Link-State NLRIs and in the BGP-LS Attribute is encoded in Type/Length/Value triplets. The TLV format applies to both the NLRI and the BGP-LS Attribute encodings. The Length field defines the length of the value portion in octets, so a TLV with no value portion has a length of zero. The TLV is not padded to 4-octet alignment.

Unknown and unsupported types MUST be preserved and propagated within both the NLRI and the BGP-LS Attribute, and the presence of unknown or unexpected TLVs MUST NOT result in the NLRI or the BGP-LS Attribute being considered malformed. An example of an unexpected TLV is one received along with an update for a link-state object other than the one that the TLV is specified as associated with.

To compare NLRIs with unknown TLVs, all TLVs within the NLRI MUST be ordered in ascending order by TLV Type. If there are multiple TLVs of the same type within a single NLRI, the TLVs sharing the same type MUST be first in ascending order based on the Length field, followed by ascending order based on the Value field. Comparison of the Value fields treats the entire field as opaque binary data and orders it lexicographically. NLRIs whose TLVs do not follow these ordering rules MUST be considered malformed by a BGP-LS Propagator. This insistence on canonical ordering prevents multiple variant copies of the same NLRI from multiple Producers and the ambiguity arising therefrom.

For both the NLRI and BGP-LS Attribute parts, all TLVs are considered optional except where explicitly specified as mandatory or required in specific conditions. The TLVs within the BGP-LS Attribute SHOULD be ordered in ascending order by TLV type, but an attribute with unordered TLVs MUST NOT be considered malformed.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is written as a small box: a number saying what it is, a number saying how long the contents are, and the contents. A box the reader does not recognise is passed on rather than thrown away, so that new information can be added later without breaking older equipment. The boxes have to be in a fixed order, so that two copies of the same thing compare equal.

sections.title: The Link-State NLRI
sections.content:
The MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes are BGP's containers for carrying opaque information. This specification defines three Link-State NLRI types that describe either a node, a link or a prefix. All non-VPN link, node and prefix information SHALL be encoded using AFI 16388 and SAFI 71. VPN link, node and prefix information SHALL be encoded using AFI 16388 and SAFI 72. For two BGP Speakers to exchange Link-State NLRI, they MUST use the BGP Capabilities Advertisement to ensure that both are capable of properly processing such NLRI, using capability code 1 with AFI 16388 and SAFI 71 for BGP-LS and AFI 16388 and SAFI 72 for BGP-LS-VPN.

Each Link-State NLRI begins with an NLRI Type and a Total NLRI Length, followed by the NLRI itself, and for VPN applications a Route Distinguisher of 8 octets. The four NLRI types are Node NLRI, Link NLRI, IPv4 Topology Prefix NLRI and IPv6 Topology Prefix NLRI. Each carries a Protocol-ID and an 8-octet Identifier, then descriptors.

The Protocol-ID says where the information came from: IS-IS Level 1, IS-IS Level 2, OSPFv2, Direct, Static configuration or OSPFv3. The Direct and Static configuration protocol types SHOULD be used when BGP-LS is sourcing local information; the Protocol-ID Direct SHOULD be used if BGP-LS has direct access to interface information and wants to advertise a local link, and Static configuration SHOULD be used for modelling virtual links.

The Identifier field carries an 8-octet BGP-LS Instance Identifier used to identify the IGP routing domain where the NLRI belongs, so that NLRIs representing objects from the same IGP routing instance have the same value. The BGP-LS Instance-ID 0 is RECOMMENDED when there is only a single protocol instance in the network where BGP-LS is operational, and the network operator MUST assign the same Instance-IDs on all Producers within a given IGP domain.

Each Node, Link and Prefix Descriptor consists of one or more TLVs. The Local Node Descriptors TLV, whose type is 256, is mandatory in all three NLRI types. The Remote Node Descriptors TLV, whose type is 257, is mandatory for Link NLRIs. The Link Descriptor TLVs uniquely identify a link among multiple parallel links between a pair of anchor routers. A link described this way is a half-link, a unidirectional representation; two anchor routers advertise a half-link each, and a link is not considered complete unless both halves are described.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of thing that can be published: a router, one direction of a link, an IPv4 prefix and an IPv6 prefix. Each one says which routing protocol it came from, which instance of that protocol, and enough identifiers to be unambiguous. A link is published twice, once from each end, and only counts as present when both halves arrive.

sections.title: The BGP-LS Attribute
sections.content:
The BGP-LS Attribute, assigned value 29 by IANA, is an optional, non-transitive BGP Attribute used to carry link, node and prefix parameters and attributes. It is defined as a set of Type/Length/Value triplets and SHOULD only be included with Link-State NLRIs. The Node Attribute TLVs, Link Attribute TLVs and Prefix Attribute TLVs are sets of TLVs that may be encoded in the attribute associated with a Node NLRI, a Link NLRI and a Prefix NLRI respectively.

The size of the BGP-LS Attribute may grow large, depending on the amount of link-state information associated with a single NLRI. The BGP specification mandates a maximum BGP message size of 4096 octets, and it is RECOMMENDED that implementations support the extended message size for BGP to accommodate a larger size of information. Producers MUST ensure that the TLVs included in the attribute do not result in a BGP UPDATE message for a single Link-State NLRI that crosses the maximum limit for a BGP message.

Among the Node Attribute TLVs are the Node Flag Bits, whose value is a one-octet bit array of flags, where each bit represents a node-operational state or attribute: the Overload bit, the Attached bit, the External bit, the ABR bit, the Router bit and the V6 bit. The bits that are not defined MUST be set to 0 by the originator and MUST be ignored by the receiver. Other node attributes include the Opaque Node Attribute, the Node Name, whose maximum length is 255 octets and whose value is encoded in 7-bit ASCII, the IS-IS Area Identifier, and the local IPv4 and IPv6 Router-ID TLVs used to describe auxiliary Router-IDs that the IGP might be using.
sections.plainLanguage: The routes themselves say which object they describe. A second BGP attribute, attached to the same route, carries the properties: the metric, the bandwidth, the node's flags such as whether it is overloaded, and its name. Because BGP messages have a size limit, a producer has to keep this part within the limit.

sections.title: Aggregating Links Into Paths
sections.content:
Distribution of all links available on the global Internet is certainly possible; however, it is not desirable from a scaling and privacy point of view. Therefore, an implementation may support a link to path aggregation. Rather than advertising all specific links of a domain, an ASBR may advertise an aggregate link between a non-adjacent pair of nodes. The aggregate link represents the aggregated set of link properties between that pair of nodes. The actual methods to compute the path properties, of bandwidth and metric, are outside the scope of the document, and the decision of whether to advertise all specific links or aggregated links is an operator's policy choice.

The document gives three deployment examples. With no link aggregation, both AS1 and AS2 operators want to protect their inter-AS links with RSVP Fast Reroute LSPs, so if R1 wants to compute its link-protection LSP to R3 it needs to see an alternate path to R3. The AS2 operator therefore exposes its topology, and all BGP-TE-enabled routers in AS1 see the full topology of AS2 and can compute a backup path.

With ASBR to ASBR path aggregation, no specific link gets exposed. The only link advertised by AS2 is an aggregate link between R3 and R4, which is enough to tell AS1 that there is a backup path, while the actual links being used are hidden from the topology. With multi-AS path aggregation, a service provider in control of multiple ASes may decide not to expose its internal inter-AS links at all, and the whole AS3 is modelled as a single node connected to the border routers of the aggregated domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing every link is easy but gives away the shape of the network and does not scale. Instead, an operator can publish one summary link between two border routers instead of every internal link, and a neighbouring network still learns that a backup path exists without learning the internal structure.

sections.title: Running BGP-LS in a Network
sections.content:
Existing BGP operational procedures apply and no new operation procedures are defined. The NLRI information carries purely application-level data that has no immediate impact on the forwarding state computed by BGP, so any churn in reachability information has a different impact than regular BGP updates, which need to change the forwarding state for an entire router. Distribution of the BGP-LS NLRIs SHOULD be handled by dedicated route reflectors in most deployments, providing a level of isolation and fault containment between different BGP address families. In the event of dedicated route reflectors not being available, other mechanisms such as separation of BGP instances or separate BGP sessions SHOULD be used.

It is RECOMMENDED that operators deploying BGP-LS enable two or more BGP-LS Producers in each IGP flooding domain to achieve redundancy in the origination of link-state information into BGP-LS. It is also RECOMMENDED that operators ensure redundancy in the BGP update propagation paths, for example using at least a pair of route reflectors, and ensure that BGP-LS Consumers are receiving the topology information from at least two BGP-LS Speakers.

Configuration parameters SHOULD be initialized to default values: the Link-State NLRI capability is turned off for all neighbors, and the maximum rate at which Link-State NLRIs will be advertised or withdrawn from neighbors is set to 200 updates per second. The extension is only activated between BGP peers after capability negotiation, and it can be turned on or off on an individual peer basis, so it can be gradually rolled out in the network. The frequency of Link-State NLRI updates could interfere with regular BGP prefix distribution, and distribution of BGP-LS NLRIs SHOULD be limited to a single administrative domain, which can consist of multiple areas within an AS or multiple ASes.
sections.plainLanguage: Running this alongside ordinary BGP needs care, because a busy topology feed can crowd out the routing traffic. The document recommends separate route reflectors for the topology feed, two producers in each area so that there is a backup, and starting with the feature switched off on every neighbour so that it can be enabled one peer at a time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Procedures and protocol extensions defined in this document do not affect the BGP security model. The operator should ensure that a BGP-LS Speaker does not accept UPDATE messages from a peer that only provides information to a BGP-LS Consumer, by using the policy configuration options described in the document. Generally, an operator is aware of the BGP-LS Speaker's role and link-state peerings, and can therefore protect the BGP-LS Speaker from peers sending updates that may represent erroneous information, feedback loops or false input.

An error or tampering of the link-state information that is originated into BGP-LS and propagated through the network can result in the malfunction of the consumer applications. Examples of such risks are the origination of incorrect information that is not present or consistent with the IGP LSDB at the Producer, incorrect ordering of TLVs in the NLRI, or inconsistent origination from multiple Producers and updates to either the NLRI or the BGP-LS Attribute during propagation, including discarding due to errors. These are not new risks from a BGP perspective; however, in the case of BGP-LS the impact reflects on the consumer applications instead of BGP routing functionalities.

Additionally, it may be considered that the export of link-state and TE information constitutes a risk to the confidentiality of mission-critical or commercially sensitive information about the network. BGP peerings are not automatic and require configuration, so it is the responsibility of the network operator to ensure that only trusted BGP Speakers are configured to receive such information.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad topology data does not break routing, but it does break the tools that plan paths from it. The document therefore says to control carefully which peers may send link-state information, and to be aware that the topology you publish describes your network in enough detail to be sensitive.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value portion in octets. A TLV with no value has a length of zero. The value follows and is not padded.

fields.name: NLRI Type
fields.desc: 1 for a node, 2 for a link, 3 for an IPv4 prefix and 4 for an IPv6 prefix.

fields.name: Total NLRI Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the rest of the NLRI, not counting the type field or itself.

items.label: Node NLRI
items.desc: Describes a node, with its local node descriptors.

items.label: Link NLRI
items.desc: Describes one direction of a link, with local and remote node descriptors and link descriptors.

items.label: IPv4 Topology Prefix NLRI
items.desc: Describes an IPv4 prefix advertised by a node.

items.label: IPv6 Topology Prefix NLRI
items.desc: Describes an IPv6 prefix advertised by a node.
